caption:
Was the Cardiff Giant real? No — and the man who made it wanted you to know.

On October 16, 1869, two men hired to dig a well behind William Newell's barn in Cardiff, New York, struck a ten-foot stone figure. One of them reportedly said, "I declare, some old Indian has been buried here!"

It was a fake. George Hull, a New York tobacconist and a skeptic, had lost an argument at a Methodist revival about the giants in Genesis 6:4. He set out to prove how easily people could be fooled. In 1868 he had a block of gypsum quarried at Fort Dodge, Iowa — telling the workmen it was for a Lincoln monument — shipped it to a Chicago stonecutter, and had it carved to imitate his own body. He learned from a geologist that hair does not petrify, so the giant has none. Sulphuric acid aged the surface. Steel knitting needles set in a board punched the pores.

Newell charged fifty cents for fifteen minutes. Three to five hundred people came a day. Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh saw soluble gypsum carrying fresh tool marks and called it "a most decided humbug." Cornell's Andrew D. White simply asked why anyone would dig a well there. Hull confessed on December 10, 1869.

What is not settled: whether Edward Burkhardt, the Chicago stonecutter, knew what he was carving. The record only notes that quilts were hung to muffle the sound.

Images: Bain News Service negative of the giant, 1910; "The Onondaga Giant" lithograph, Popular Graphic Arts; and both sides of an 1873 stereocard of the Fort Dodge gypsum quarry, from the New York Public Library.
